newsitem.title: USA: Exports, tight supplies boost CBOT rice futures.
newsitem.headline: Exports, tight supplies boost CBOT rice futures.

text.p: Rice futures on the Chicago Board of Trade ended sharply higher on Thursday, buoyed by fund buying, tight U.S. supplies and strong exports, analysts said.
Rice futures have risen steadily since December 23, when March rice closed strong at $10.99. On Thursday, March ended up the 30-cent daily limit at $12.39 per hundredweight, a new contract high.

"The market has just been going up, up and up, and the cash seems to be following it," said Neauman Coleman, Dean Witter Reynolds senior vice president, futures. "They play leapfrog with one another."
Analysts said the market was being underpinned by strong export demand for long grain rice and tight domestic supply.
"We are seeing a market to some extent driven by exports of U.S. rough rice going to the central and southern Latin American countries," Coleman said.
He said demand has caused a tight supply situation for U.S. mills who need to buy rice for their domestic needs.
"For the first time in months, there are a few milled rice inquiries in the market," Creed Rice Market Report publisher Mark Creed wrote in his latest weekly report.

"Iraq is in the market for 30,000 tonnes of U.S. long grain milled 10 percent brokens (on February 3). Also, Nicaragua and Dominican Republic are inquiring about 5,000 tonnes each for no.2/4 Long Grain Hard Milled," Creed said.

The U.S. Department of Agriculture early Thursday said U.S. net export sales of rice totalled 70,500 tonnes in the week ended January 23. That was 42 percent below the previous week but 29 percent above the four-week average sales pace.
Export sales for the current marketing year that started on August 1, 1996, totalled 574,800 tonnes against 425,500 at the same time last year, according to USDA data.
Rice Market Advisory Letter publisher J.P. Gaines said there was unexpected large demand coming from Guatemala.
"They have reported buying 26,000 tonnes of U.S. long grain rough rice over the past three weeks," Gaines said.

He also pointed to larger than usual demand from Saudi Arabia, possibly the result of sharply increased prices for India's parboiled basmati rice. "The Saudis also purchased about 30,000 tonnes of long grain parboiled U.S. rice over the past three weeks," Gaines said.
Analysts said the boost in export demand came in the face of a U.S. long grain rice crop expected to be as as much as 10 percent smaller this year.
On January 10, USDA estimated U.S. long grain rice output in the current 1996/97 (August/July) year would fall to 113.4 million cwt compared to 121.7 million a year earlier.
"Most people in the industry believe the USDA's estimate was on the high side," Gaines said.
